segments.translit: /don de nyid bde ba chen po'i rgyal po chos thams cad dmigs pa med pa'i ro de yis slar yang nag po spyod pa pa rnam par sgom par byed do/
segments.translation: With that taste of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all [dharmas]{dharma}, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} once again thoroughly [meditates]{bhavana} on that very meaning, the king of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.
segments.note: Munidatta, in the Tibetan, opens by saying that [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, with the taste of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all things, once again meditates on that very meaning, 'the king of [great bliss]{mahasukha}' (cp.24.m1). The verb, rnam par sgom pa, may stand for a Sanskrit word meaning 'set forth'; the Sanskrit is lost.

flags.note: Munidatta's comment on song 24 survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); the Sanskrit original is lost and this is a translation of the Tibetan. The Sanskrit behind 'king of great bliss' (perhaps *mahāsukharāja), 'non-apprehension' (perhaps *anupalambha, as the glossary records at cp.06.m2) and the verb can be inferred only through the Tibetan. I checked the machine Wylie against the script: no corrections needed.

rnam par sgom par byed literally means 'thoroughly meditates on, cultivates'. It is the regular Tibetan for Sanskrit vibhāvayati, which in commentators' openings often means 'sets forth, makes clear'. I kept the Tibetan's literal sense ('meditates on', glossary bhavana). If the reviewer reads it as the Sanskrit idiom, 'sets forth' would replace it, without the bhavana link.

I take 'the king of great bliss' as standing in apposition to 'that very meaning' (the glossary's entry for Kukkurīpāda has Munidatta set out 'the king of great bliss' at cp.02.m1). Another reading takes it with what follows: 'by that king of great bliss, the taste of the non-apprehension of all dharmas'. ro de yis ('by that taste') may also have lost a participle such as 'drunk on' or 'delighted by'.
nag po spyod pa pa renders Kṛṣṇācārya, the name Munidatta uses in Sanskrit. I rendered it 'Kāṇha' as glossary p-kanha requires; see questions.

segments.translit: /zla ba gang ba zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni bla ma'i drin las gang gi dus su cha bcu drug dang ldan pa'i byang chub kyi sems kyi zla ba'i dkyil 'khor shar bar gyur pa de'i dus su rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug sems kyi rgyal po shin du dri ma med par 'gyur ro/
segments.translation: 'The [full moon]{full-moon}' and so on: at the time when, by the [guru]{guru}'s [grace]{prasada}, the [moon]{moon} [maṇḍala]{mandala} of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, endowed with [sixteen digits]{sixteen-digits}, has risen, at that time the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, becomes utterly free of [stain]{mala}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [full moon]{full-moon} as the [moon]{moon} [maṇḍala]{mandala} ('disc') of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} ('mind of awakening'), complete with its [sixteen digits]{sixteen-digits}, which rises by the [guru]{guru}'s [grace]{prasada}; at that time the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, becomes utterly free of [stain]{mala} (cp.24.m2).

equations.en: the moon maṇḍala of bodhicitta, endowed with sixteen digits, risen by the guru's grace
the lord of yogis (named in apposition, not in an 'X means Y' gloss)

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293). The original is lost and this translates the Tibetan. The Sanskrit behind zla ba'i dkyil 'khor (perhaps *candramaṇḍala), cha bcu drug (perhaps *ṣoḍaśakalā), rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug (*yogīndra) and drin (*prasāda) can be inferred only through the Tibetan.
The source writes ཤིན་དུ shin du for the usual shin tu, 'utterly'. I transliterated it as written. The sense is not affected.

I rendered dkyil 'khor as 'maṇḍala', as the glossary requires. In this compound (zla ba'i dkyil 'khor) 'moon-disc' is plainer English, and the glossary's own entries for full-moon and king-of-mind use it. See questions.

segments.translit: /d+hA'i rkang pa don de nyid brtan par byed do/ /gcod pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni blo gros dang ldan pas bla ma'i gsung gis gti mug la sogs pa'i sgrib pa 'bros par 'gyur ro/ /yul dang dbang po zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni nam mkhar 'od gsal la 'jug par byed do/ /de bzhin du sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis kyang / dus mnyam shar ba de la phyag 'tshal lo/ /zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs so/
segments.translation: The [refrain]{dhruvapada} makes that very meaning firm. 'Cuts' and so on: for one endowed with [intelligence]{mati}, by the [guru]{guru}'s word the [obscurations]{avarana} of [delusion]{moha} and the rest flee. '[Sense objects]{visaya} and [senses]{indriya}' and so on: they enter into the [sky]{gagana}, into [clear light]{prabhasvara}. In the same way [Saraha]{p-saraha}pāda too said, 'I bow to that which has risen at the same time,' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta says the [refrain]{dhruvapada} makes the same meaning firm: for one endowed with intelligence, the [obscurations]{avarana} of [delusion]{moha} and the rest flee by the [guru]{guru}'s word, and [sense objects]{visaya} and [senses]{indriya} enter 'the sky, clear light'. He adds a line of [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'I bow to that which has risen at the same time' (cp.24.m3).

equations.en: clear light (by apposition: 'into the sky, into clear light')

citations.quoted: I bow to that which has risen at the same time
citations.work: Saraha (named by Munidatta; the work is not named, perhaps a dohā collection)

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293). The original is lost and this translates the Tibetan. d+hA'i rkang pa transcribes the cue for the dhruvapada (Shastri's editions print ধ্রু): the Tibetan has dhā, perhaps a misreading of dhru. The Sanskrit behind blo gros dang ldan pa (perhaps *matimat or *dhīmat) can be inferred only through the Tibetan.

brtan par byed ('makes firm') seems to play on dhruva, 'firm', since Tibetan elsewhere renders dhruvapada as brtan pa'i rkang pa. I left it unmarked rather than linking it to sthira ('steady'), because the glossary uses that entry for yogic steadiness.

In nam mkhar 'od gsal la 'jug par byed do both nouns carry a terminative or locative ending. I took this as apposition, 'into the sky, into clear light', which would mean the sky is read as clear light; the equation is recorded on that basis. Another reading: 'enter clear light in the sky'. 'jug par byed may also be causative, with the guru's word or the intelligent one making the sense objects and senses enter.

I could not identify Saraha's line (dus mnyam shar ba de la phyag 'tshal lo). dus mnyam shar ba, 'risen at the same time', might render a word like sahaja, 'born together' (usually lhan cig skyes pa), or describe things arising together. 'Risen' echoes shar in 1a and 4a. The Apabhraṃśa original can be inferred only through the Tibetan.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gnyis pa chos kyi sa bon gyi nus pa gsungs te/ mkha' mtshungs sa bon zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni nam mkha' dang mtshungs pa'i sa bon ni 'od gsal gyi rang bzhin sems las skyes pa ste/ de'i rang bzhin 'od rab tu gsal ba ni rang gi shing ljon pa'i grib ma rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug ye shes kyi 'od zer gyis 'jig rten gsum po khyab pa'o/
segments.translation: The second [verse]{pada} teaches the power of the [seed]{seed} of [dharma]{dharma}. 'A [seed]{seed} like the [sky]{gagana}' and so on: the [seed]{seed} like the [sky]{gagana} is born from the [mind]{citta} whose nature is [clear light]{prabhasvara}; its nature, utterly luminous, is the [shade]{shade} of its own [tree]{tree}: the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} pervades the [three worlds]{trailokya} with the rays of [knowledge]{jnana}.
segments.note: Munidatta takes this verse as teaching the power of the [seed]{seed} of dharma: the sky-like seed is born from the mind whose nature is [clear light]{prabhasvara}; the [shade]{shade} of its own tree is its utterly luminous nature, and the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} pervades the three worlds with rays of [knowledge]{jnana} (cp.24.m4).

equations.en: the seed of dharma, born from the mind whose nature is clear light

equations.src: rang gi shing ljon pa'i grib ma

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293). The original is lost and this translates the Tibetan. The Sanskrit behind chos kyi sa bon (perhaps *dharmabīja), 'od gsal gyi rang bzhin sems (perhaps *prabhāsvarasvabhāvacitta) and ye shes kyi 'od zer (perhaps *jñānaraśmi; compare the Sanskrit at cp.19.m4 recorded under yoginijala) can be inferred only through the Tibetan. The comment has 'jig rten gsum po where the song has khams gsum; both are rendered 'three worlds'.

I read 'od gsal gyi rang bzhin sems las skyes pa as 'born from the mind whose nature is clear light', as the glossary entry for seed does. It can also be divided as 'is of the nature of clear light, born from the mind'.

de'i rang bzhin ('its nature') may refer to the seed or to the mind. The final clause, 'the lord of yogis pervades the three worlds with the rays of knowledge', is attached without a connective. The comment does not say whether the lord of yogis is the tree, the shade or the one who pervades.
'od rab tu gsal ba ('utterly luminous') is the full form of 'od gsal and may render the same Sanskrit prabhāsvara ('clear light'). I translated it literally and left it unmarked.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gsum pas de'i khyad par gyi mtshan nyid gsungs te/ mtshan mo sel zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni dper na nyin mor byed pa shar bar gyur na mtshan mo mun pa sel ba bzhin du ji ltar bla ma dam pa'i zhabs kyi rdul gyi tshogs la rab tu 'dud na so sor lta ba las yang dag par skyes pa'i rang bzhin gyi drin las srid pa'i rgya mtshor ye shes kyi gti mug dang zhe sdang la sogs pa'i sgrib pa ring du 'gros par gsungs so/
segments.translation: The third [verse]{pada} teaches its distinguishing characteristic. 'Clears away the [night]{night}' and so on: for example, just as, when the [sun]{surya} has risen, it clears away the darkness of [night]{night}, so, when one bows low to the mass of dust on the feet of the true [guru]{guru}, then by the [grace]{prasada} of the nature that has truly arisen from discerning examination, the [delusion]{moha}, [hatred]{dvesa} and other [obscurations]{avarana} of [knowledge]{jnana} go far away in the [ocean]{ocean} of [existence]{bhava}. This is what it teaches.
segments.note: Munidatta explains the verse by example: as the rising [sun]{surya} clears away the darkness of night, so for one who bows low to the dust of the true [guru]{guru}'s feet, [delusion]{moha}, [hatred]{dvesa} and the other [obscurations]{avarana} 'of knowledge' go far away in the ocean of existence, by the grace of a nature born from discerning examination (cp.24.m5).

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293). The original is lost and this translates the Tibetan. The Sanskrit behind nyin mor byed pa ('day-maker', perhaps *divākara, rendered 'sun' as in the draft), bla ma dam pa'i zhabs kyi rdul (perhaps *sadgurucaraṇareṇu) and so sor lta ba (perhaps *pratyavekṣaṇā) can be inferred only through the Tibetan.

ye shes kyi ('of knowledge') before 'delusion, hatred and the rest' is hard, since knowledge is not normally said to have delusion and hatred as its obscurations. It may reflect a Sanskrit *ajñāna- ('ignorance') read as jñāna after a word ending in -e (*bhavasāgare 'jñāna-), where the avagraha is often left unwritten. This can be inferred only through the Tibetan. I translated the Tibetan as it stands. Another possibility is 'obscurations to knowledge'.

so sor lta ba las yang dag par skyes pa'i rang bzhin gyi drin las is obscure. I rendered it 'by the grace of the nature that has truly arisen from discerning examination'. so sor lta ba may render pratyavekṣaṇā, as in the 'discerning' wisdom, and rang bzhin gyi drin may mean 'by grace, naturally' rather than 'by the grace of the nature'.
ring du 'gros par probably stands for 'gro bar ('go far') or for 'bros par ('flee far', the word m3 uses). I transliterated 'gros as written; the sense is the same.
ji ltar, coming after bzhin du in the middle of the simile, is redundant. I took it as 'so'.

segments.translit: /rkang pa bzhi pas rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug gi spyod pa gsungs te/ ngang pa'i rgyal po zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni dper na phyi rol du ngang pa'i rgyal pos chu dang 'o ma 'dres pa'i chu rnam par phye nas 'o ma 'thung bar byed do/ /nag po spyod pa nyid la kye'i rnal 'byor pa mchog gi de nyid kyis srid pa'i rang bzhin khong du chud pas srid pa bza' bar bya ba yin gyis khyod srid pa len par ma byed cig pa'o/ /de bzhin du/ ye shes byang chub pa las kyang / /srid pa ma yin myang 'das min/ /yang dag ji bzhin rtogs pa las/ /zhes so/
segments.translation: The fourth [verse]{pada} teaches the [conduct]{carya} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}. 'The [swan king]{swan-king}' and so on: for example, outwardly, the [swan king]{swan-king} separates water in which water and milk are mixed, and drinks the milk. To [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} himself: 'O supreme [yogi]{yogi}, once the nature of [existence]{bhava} has been understood through reality itself, [existence]{bhava} is to be eaten; but you must not take [existence]{bhava} up.' In the same way the [Jñānasaṃbodhi]{tx-jnanasambodhi} too says: 'It is not [existence]{bhava}, it is not [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}; / from realizing the real just as it is…'
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse teaches the [conduct]{carya} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}. Outwardly, the [swan king]{swan-king} separates water mixed with milk and drinks the milk; so [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} is told, as supreme yogi, to eat existence once its nature is understood through reality, but not to take it up. A verse of the Jñānasaṃbodhi follows (cp.24.m6).

citations.quoted: It is not existence, it is not nirvāṇa; / from realizing the real just as it is…

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293). The original is lost and this translates the Tibetan. The comment quotes the song's word as ngang pa'i rgyal po, which supports emending dang pa'i rgyal pos in 5a to 'swan king', as the draft does. kye'i renders the Sanskrit vocative he, as in kye'i rdo rje for Hevajra. Sanskrit for the swan king (perhaps *haṃsarāja) and the rest can be inferred only through the Tibetan.

In kye'i rnal 'byor pa mchog gi de nyid kyis, the genitive gi after a vocative is unexpected. I read it as 'O supreme yogi ... through reality itself' (de nyid as tattva). Other readings: 'through the reality of the supreme yogi', or gi as a slip for gis, giving 'by the supreme yogi himself' as agent of 'is to be eaten'.

The comment turns 5b's 'eats existence' into an instruction ('existence is to be eaten; but you must not take existence up') and addresses Kāṇha as 'you'. The draft line ('so one eats existence') stays as it is; I have noted the difference rather than harmonizing.

I took ye shes byang chub pa las kyang as the title (Jñānasaṃbodhi, glossary tx-jnanasambodhi), following the usual de bzhin du [title] las kyang formula. It is also seven syllables and could be read as a first verse line ('even from awakening in knowledge'). The quotation stops after its third line, so it is incomplete.

questions: Commentary name: m1 and m6 have nag po spyod pa (pa), i.e. Kṛṣṇācārya, the name Munidatta uses in Sanskrit, not the song's kAh+Na. As glossary p-kanha requires, I rendered it 'Kāṇha'. Should 'Kṛṣṇācārya' be allowed as a variant inside the commentary?
m1: should rnam par sgom par byed be rendered literally ('meditates on', linked to bhavana), as I did, or as the Sanskrit idiom it probably renders (vibhāvayati, 'sets forth')?

m5: ye shes kyi gti mug dang zhe sdang ('the delusion, hatred ... of knowledge') reads oddly. Do you accept the literal rendering, or would you note the conjecture that the translators read *ajñāna ('ignorance') as jñāna after bhavasāgare?
m3: can you identify Saraha's line 'dus mnyam shar ba de la phyag 'tshal lo' ('I bow to that which has risen at the same time')? Is dus mnyam shar ba perhaps a rendering of sahaja?
m2: for zla ba'i dkyil 'khor I wrote 'moon maṇḍala', as the glossary requires. May 'moon-disc', the form the glossary's own entries use, be a variant of mandala in this compound?

m3: I read nam mkhar 'od gsal la as apposition ('into the sky, into clear light') and recorded an equation of sky with clear light. If you agree, the gagana entry could gain this reading (cp.24.m3); if you read 'clear light in the sky', the equation should go.
m4: should 'od rab tu gsal ba ('utterly luminous'), the full form of 'od gsal, be linked to prabhasvara ('clear light')? I left it literal and unmarked.
